survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This factsheet reports PISA 2022 results for Guatemala using OECD’s PISA 2022 Database and published tables (e.g., I.B1.* and II.B1.*). The document does not specify the exact student sampling weight variable name or whether replicate weights (e.g., BRR/jackknife) were applied in the computations shown. Because this is an OECD results factsheet rather than a re-analysis paper, the weighting and variance estimation procedures are assumed to follow PISA’s standard complex survey design methodology used to produce the reported means, confidence intervals, and proficiency-level shares. Analysts using the underlying PISA microdata should apply the official PISA sampling weights and replicate weights provided in the database when estimating standard errors and confidence intervals for Guatemala and any subgroups (e.g., ESCS quintiles, gender).

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This document is a descriptive results factsheet that reports proficiency-level shares and mean performance using OECD’s already-produced PISA estimates, rather than providing an explicit student-level modeling workflow with documented PV combination and missing-data procedures. Plausible values are therefore not handled in a way that is transparent at the factsheet level (the underlying OECD scaling/PV methodology is encapsulated in the published database tables). Missing-data handling is likewise not described because the factsheet focuses on reporting final PISA estimates rather than detailing the imputation/deletion strategy used to construct them.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used the PISA 2022 assessment sample for Guatemala that completed the mathematics, reading, or science assessment (paper-and-pencil test) in 290 schools; the factsheet reports 5,190 students completing the assessment in mathematics, reading or science. The document does not provide additional analytic exclusions (e.g., missing background questionnaire items) beyond the standard PISA data quality and reporting standards; it states that all Guatemala data met PISA quality standards and were fit for reporting.

data.outcome_summary: This OECD PISA 2022 factsheet summarizes how 15-year-old students in Guatemala performed in mathematics, reading, and science, and how results changed relative to Guatemala’s first participation in 2017. The assessment used a two-hour paper-and-pencil test with multiple-choice and constructed-response items, plus a student background questionnaire and a school principal questionnaire. The factsheet reports mean performance comparisons to the OECD average, proficiency-level shares (e.g., Level 2+ and Level 5/6), and trends in performance from 2017 to 2022, including changes (or lack thereof) in gaps between top and bottom deciles and in the proportion below Level 2. It also highlights within-country disparities by ESCS (socioeconomic status), gender differences, and contextual indicators such as belonging, discipline in mathematics lessons, safety, parental involvement, and COVID-related learning experiences. Methodologically, it is a descriptive reporting product: it does not present an original ML modeling pipeline or explicit PV/missing-data handling steps at the factsheet level.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This is an OECD PISA results factsheet rather than an empirical research article estimating predictive models. As a result, there is no student-level ML algorithm training/evaluation, no explicit PV-combination or missing-data handling procedure described in the text, and no analytic sample construction details beyond the reported PISA participation sample and quality-fit statement. The absence of main_findings rows and confounders reflects that the document reports official PISA estimates and descriptive comparisons rather than testing hypotheses with a specified statistical/ML design.
